https://www.politico.eu/article/zack-pol.text: LONDON — Zack Polanski promised to smash Britain’s two-party political system — but his campaign for a U.K. parliamentary seat has leaned heavily on the idea that he can keep the existing prime minister honest. POLITICO analysis of the online battleground in the Holborn and St. Pancras by-election – which takes place Thursday — shows the Green leader has been pitching himself as a protest vote for Labour-backing constituents in the London seat, which has been held by Labour since its creation in 1983. The party has spent nearly £5,000 pushing ads on Meta’s platforms, which include Facebook and Instagram, promising that a Green win would help “keep the government in check.” Advertisement In one campaign video, Polanski takes credit for a series of Labour U-turns on their “most unpopular policies” over the last 12 months. A victory in the seat, he claims, would add further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to listen to the Greens, rather than “Nigel Farage, Donald Trump, or their corporate donors.” An additional £7,000 has been spent by the party promoting graphics of recent newspaper headlines it thinks demonstrate the influence it holds over Burnham’s Labour government — including a Guardian story flagging a possible delay on North Sea gas field decisions until after the by-election. “When Zack Polanski speaks, Labour listens. That is the power of the leader of the Green Party,” the accompanying ad copy states. Building Brand Zack The by-election marks Polanski’s first attempt to win a seat in the House of Commons. The left-wing leader oversaw a rapid polling increase for the Greens after taking charge in September 2025, snatching a Labour safe seat in Gorton and Denton under former Labour Prime Minister Keir Starmer the following February. But its polling momentum appears to have stalled since Labour switched to Burnham, and the party has also faced internal rows over anti-semitism. Advertisement The party has spent around £8,000 on targeted ads highlighting endorsements for Polanski from local residents, including former independent candidates and NHS workers. And at least £500 of that has been spent promoting effusive praise of the Green leader from his own local hairdresser. Alongside a picture of the pair hugging, barber Rami is quoted saying: “I’ve been cutting Zack’s hair for years. When you chat to him you can tell how much he really cares.” A significant number of the showcased endorsements come from former Labour backers and members as Polanski seeks to convince voters that Burnham’s majority — and the mid-term timing of the contest — means they can register a protest vote in the symbolic seat previously held by Starmer. One standalone advert features former Labour member Gopa, who says: “We all know there will still be a Labour government whoever wins, so I’m excited for a Green candidate who will listen to us and help push Labour to do better.” Other endorsements include a Labour member of three decades who says she is now backing Polanski after her former party “lost its way and let me down.” Ex-Labour councillor Naser says he’s switched his allegiance to “keep the pressure on, and keep Labour in check.” The Labour pitch By contrast, Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali has kept her campaign local. She has spent more than £21,000 with Meta promoting dozens of slick cinematic clips and polished graphics pitching herself as a “local champion.” Supported by Labour’s well-oiled digital team, Abdi-Wali’s online campaign focuses heavily on her experience of arriving in the area as a child refugee, and her subsequent career as a local councillor. Labour has also pumped more than £20,000 into Google’s ad program. The majority of that sum was spent on bitesize YouTube ads, with the remainder spent on buying up sponsored Google search results in an attempt to grab the attention of voters hunting for information about the contest. Also running Britain’s hard-right Restore Britain has also been making a pitch to voters in Holborn and St Pancras — while openly admitting it has no chance of winning in “one of the most left-wing seats in Britain.” Rupert Lowe’s party has spent around £30,000 on Meta ads positioning itself as a “genuine patriotic alternative” to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK — which has not spent significant cash in the contest. Restore’s spending included £1,500 promoting a “quiz” comparing comments from Reform politicians with Restore’s more hard-line agenda. A further £2,000 went on promoting a graphic of the “ten reasons” why voters should support it. Advertisement That list includes removing “millions of foreign nationals who hate who we are,” a promise to “reverse the Islamification” of London, deport “foreign tramps who ruin our city” and force “healthy” benefit claimants to clean graffiti and pick litter. In a further attempt to present his insurgent party as a credible alternative to Reform or the Conservatives, Lowe’s paid online content repeatedly describes the by-election as a “free hit” for right-wing voters to “vote with your heart.” “They don’t want the capital reformed, or conserved,” one paid ad states. “They want London restored.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip when they were shot dead. Photograph: AAP View image in fullscreen Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip when they were shot dead. Photograph: AAP Mexico Three men found guilty of murders of Australian surfer brothers and US friend in Mexico Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, 30 and 33, and friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were killed on a surfing trip in 2024 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Agence France-Press Fri 9 Oct 2026 17.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Mexican judge has convicted three men of the 2024 murders of two Australian surfers and their American friend in a case that sparked international outrage. Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery. The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States. Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. He and two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were found guilty on Friday local time. Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, traveled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September. “They took our sons from our lives forever,” said Debra Robinson, who testified on the final day of the trial. “What hurts us most is that, in their final hours, they were treated with such cruelty.” Addressing the court at the start of the trial, Martin Robinson described his sons’ murders as “hell”. “It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons,” he said. Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his fiance, Natalie Weirtz, also participated in the hearing in a video call from the United States. “The accused are guilty and must be punished so that no other family suffers the same pain,” Weirtz said. “Since Carter’s death, I feel paranoid and isolated.” The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads. Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast. Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman , were killed in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned. https://www.keyc.com/2026/10/01/doj-char.text: Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google WASHINGTON, D.C. (KEYC) - Ten foreign nationals living in Minnesota have been charged in federal court with voting illegally or lying about their citizenship to register to vote, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. Federal law strictly limits voting in federal and state elections to U.S. citizens. Prosecutors say all 10 defendants are lawful permanent residents — green card holders — but not citizens, which makes it illegal for them to register or cast a ballot. The alleged incidents took place across three recent elections: the November 2022 and 2024 general elections, as well as Minnesota’s August 2026 primary. How Did This Happen? To vote in Minnesota, a person must swear under penalty of perjury that they are a United States citizen. Federal authorities say nine of the defendants falsely checked that box or signed forms claiming citizenship, while others simply cast ballots when they were not legally allowed to do so. “The law is clear: only American citizens may vote in American elections,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. “Enforcing this law is fundamental to our democracy.” Homeland Security Investigations led the inquiry into each case. Who Was Charged? Each person was indicted separately by a grand jury and has appeared in court: Joshua Frederick Kofi Edzie, 63 (Ghana): Accused of voting illegally in the Aug. 11, 2026, Minnesota primary, and falsely claiming citizenship in both 2024 and 2026. Bhator Konah Bryant, 61 (Liberia): Accused of falsely claiming to be a citizen when registering to vote in October 2024. Edvile Vaidoto Edmunds, 59 (Lithuania): Accused of casting an illegal ballot in the November 2022 general election. Paul Kras, 78 (Germany): Accused of voting illegally in the November 2024 general election. Six others — Alan Barbu Kargbo, 48 (Liberia) , Fadil Rasim Ozegovic, 58 (Bosnia) , Aparecido Donizetti Padovan, 62 (Brazil) , Chis Adam Pettiquoi, 43 (Liberia) , Christian Liam Schenk, 47 (Canada) , and Hester Sophia Weihmann, 69 (South Africa) — are each accused of both claiming false citizenship and casting an illegal ballot on Election Day in November 2024. What Penalties Do They Face? Under federal law: Falsely claiming U.S. citizenship to vote is a felony punishable by up to five years in prison and fines up to $250,000. Voting as a non-citizen is a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in prison and fines up to $100,000. A conviction can also trigger deportation proceedings and the loss of permanent residency status. An indictment is a formal accusation. All defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. Click here to download the KEYC News Now app or our KEYC First Alert weather app. Copyright 2026 KEYC. All rights reserved. https://cyprus-mail.com/2026/10/18/chris.text: President Nikos Christodoulides on Sunday reiterated his call for local authorities to suggest to the government “projects” to be undertaken using funds he said the Republic of Cyprus has “secured” as part of the European Union’s next multiannual financial framework, despite negotiations to devise that framework being far from over between the bloc’s 27 member states. “Our country has secured, through a combination of European funds and national financing, a total of €3.5 billion for projects across the Republic of Cyprus. The projects will be determined by cabinet in September 2027. You have ten months to bring these projects to maturity with the assistance of the district governments,” he said. He added that once those projects are approved by cabinet, they will begin to be implemented “immediately”, and said to this end that “it is, therefore, up to you to develop these projects and bring them forward to us”. The €3.5bn figure had been earlier explained by Christodoulides as being the sum of the Republic of Cyprus’ contributions to and allocations from the next multiannual financial framework, which is the EU’s long-term budget for the period covering the years between 2028 and 2034. However, that budget has not yet been agreed upon, and since Christodoulides first announced the €3.5bn figure, the Irish government last week put forward a proposal which forecasts almost €110bn less spending across the board than the Cypriot government’s own proposal, which was published in June. Three budget proposals have now been made, with the European Commission’s initial proposal, made last year, foreseeing €1.76 trillion worth of spending, while the Cypriot proposal forecast €1.73tn and the Irish proposal forecasts €1.62tn over the seven-year period. Latest EU budget proposal has €28bn less funding in cohesion, agriculture, social policy Compared to the Cypriot proposal, based on which Christodoulides likely cited the €3.5bn figure, the Irish proposal has allocated €28bn less to “heading one” which brings together policies related to cohesion, agriculture and fisheries, social, and migration policy. It is under this heading that infrastructure and social projects would be funded, with the majority of those likely falling under “national and regional partnership plans” – the EU’s allocation to member states to spend on the type of projects to which Christodoulides was largely referring. The Irish proposal foresees a little under €747bn of funding for national and regional partnership plans, whereas the Cypriot government had earlier proposed that more than €770bn be spent on them, meaning that Christodoulides’ figure was based on a budget which is around three per cent, or €23.5bn, higher than the latest formal proposal. Were the allocation to which Christodoulides was referring face a cut in line with this, the actual budget allocated to Cyprus, including the Cypriot government’s own direct contributions, could be over €100 million lower than the figure Christodoulides is citing. Christodoulides said next EU budget may be 10% smaller than first proposal Not only that, but Christodoulides admitted on Thursday that the overall multiannual financial framework may be more than 10 per cent smaller than the initial proposal submitted by the European Commission in July last year, while he was in Brussels at the week’s European Council summit, negotiating the budget with other EU leaders. With the Irish proposal having been a little over eight per cent smaller than the commission’s proposal, this would entail further cuts to planned EU spending, and possibly to the cohesion budget and to national and regional partnership plans. It is expected that the next budget proposal will be offered by European Council President Antonio Costa, who has said that he will convene an extraordinary summit of the leaders of the EU’s 27 member states on November 26 with the aim of hashing out a deal before the end of the year. Christodoulides and the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas locked in talks It is widely understood that the EU and its member states hope to reach an agreement on the multiannual financial framework by the end of this year so as to ward off the risk of elections next year in France and Poland – and the possible election of the far right in both countries – derailing efforts to reach an agreement. On this front, Christodoulides had said while in Brussels during the week that should an agreement not be reached by the end of this year, “I believe we would be sending a negative message, not only to European citizens, but to the world”. Macron will reportedly refuse to negotiate after end of year This deadline reportedly hardened during Thursday’s negotiations, with Brussels-based news website Rapporteur writing that French President Emmanuel Macron had told the other 26 leaders that France cannot agree to any budget deal after December, in view of the presidential elections being held in the country in April. It reported that holding negotiations in the first months of next year would be “too politically sensitive”. “No one is unaware of the election deadline. I want a substantial budget, but I cannot finalise it on behalf of France between January and April,” Macron reportedly said. Macron and Christodoulides However, snap elections in Spain may have put paid to hopes of an agreement by the end of this year, with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez sending his country to the polls after its parliament voted down emergency legislation aimed at stemming rising housing costs. That election will take place on November 29, with it currently appearing likely that the centre-right PP and far-right Vox party will both make gains, though Sanchez’s centre-left PSOE may still be able to form a coalition after the election. As such, Costa’s planned extraordinary meeting will take place just three days before the Spanish election. Of this, Christodoulides told Politico on Thursday night that “everybody used to understand that we need to finish a political agreement by the end of the year”, but that “now, with the situation in Spain, elections there”, this may be less possible. EU leaders reached an agreement in July last time out Should an agreement not be reached by the end of this year, matters may go to the wire, with the next French president unlikely to take office in mid-May, and it possible that the winning candidate there could change the complexion of the negotiations and the overall political character of Europe. The elections in Poland will take place in November at the latest, meaning there could be a mad dash to the finish for those negotiations, particularly with the legislation which follows the agreement typically taking months to negotiate with the European Parliament, draft, and ratify. For the last multiannual financial framework, EU leaders reached an agreement in July 2020 – five months out from its implementation – before then negotiating with the European Parliament until November, with member states then finalising their adoption of the agreed budget on December 14, 2020, and the parliament voting it through two days later.

The attack on the Kamensky plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky involved drones and Neptune missiles, according to the Ukrainian account. The military said the plant supplies fuel for ammunition used by Russia's Uragan, Smerch and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as other missiles and air-launched weapons. Edited by: Kieran Burke https://p.dw.com/p/5Otqz Skip next section Ukraine welcomes civilians from Oleshky after complex evacuation effort 10/31/2026 October 31, 2026 Ukraine welcomes civilians from Oleshky after complex evacuation effort Ukrainian officials said evacuees brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot, and a racoon Image: Genya Savilov/AFP First evacuees from the Russian-occupied Oleshky have reached Ukrainian-controlled territory amid a localized ceasefire. Oleshky, near the front line in the southern Kherson region, has been occupied by Russia since 2022. In recent weeks, the town has faced a severe humanitarian crisis. Both sides have recently agreed to a localized ceasefire to extract the estimated 2,000 civilians still in Oleshky, down from its pre-invasion population of 24,000. Moscow and Kyiv credited the US first lady, Melania Trump, with brokering the truce. Residents were given a choice to go to Russia or travel via Belarus to the part of Ukraine controlled by Kyiv. Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the initiative required "an enormous amount of work." He said evacuees included a one-year-old baby and a 94-year-old resident of Oleshky. The evacuees brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon, according to Lubinets. He expressed hope that the Oleshky arrangement can be replicated elsewhere. The truce started on Tuesday and is due to end on Sunday night.
